newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Republican rivals eye state surplus warily.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Republican rivals eye state surplus warily.

text.p: The acting governor of Massachusetts and the treasurer, rivals for the Republican nomination as governor, seem to share the same philosophy of 'once bitten, twice shy' when it comes to the state's finances.

Both see the same threat in what other elected officials, who have not seen their state's economic boom collapse, might view with less trepidation -- surging tax revenues that could give Massachusetts a $400 million surplus in fiscal 1997.

Asked to identify the biggest financial risk facing the state, Paul Cellucci, acting governor, said, "As far as I'm concerned, the greatest risk we have is government-related. The fact that we have all this surplus revenue -- if we don't cut taxes and give that surplus revenue back to the citizens of Massachusetts, then I think that it will be used to make the government bigger."

He added, "That's what happened in the 1980s, and I want to make sure that it doesn't happen to the state of Massachusetts again." Cellucci made the comments during an interview with RFTV, parts of which were scheduled to be shown at 1130 EDT Tuesday, along with an interview with the state treasurer.
Massachusetts saw its economy go off the rails in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when it was hit especially hard by the recession.

Treasurer Joe Malone, asked what he considered the biggest financial risk, replied, "The biggest risk facing Massachusetts is to make sure that simply because revenues are exceeding projections that we don't go off and spend those revenues right now."

Later, noting the state government's spending in the 1980s rose at three times the rate of inflation, he added, "Then, when there was a slowdown in the economy, that's when the real trauma hit, and I don't think anybody wants to go through that kind of traumatic experience again."

There seemed less agreement about another potential hazard -- the risk that the Central Artery project, which involves replacing an elevated highway in Boston with a depressed, eight- mile road, will cost much more than planned. The Cellucci team's ability to manage this huge construction project might prove crucial in his gubernatorial bid
One of the risks is that Washington might slash its share when in September it renews a six-year pact on transportation aid.

"I think there may be some reductions in federal spending, and obviously, that's something we're paying close attention," said Cellucci, though he noted that a new proposal includes a "hold-harmless" provision for Northeast states.

The acting governor said he was confident, however, that the $10.8 billion project would be finished on time and without cost overruns. "I don't expect there to be a shortfall," he said, though he added the state had a contingency plan.

Malone had some doubts about the issue, and called for more information, saying there was too much confusion for him to say how much spending might fall short. The General Accounting Office recently said the project would cost another $778 million because it held that the state would not get the benefit of insurance savings until 2017.

"There is a range in terms of what the federal spending will be but even with the most optimistic range, you have to wonder at the way the price is escalating, how much of a gap there will be," he said, noting the project will not be end until 2004. "There's plenty of room for price increases," he warned.

Despite this conflict, the two elected officials agree that state residents can spend the 1997 surplus more wisely than Boston; they each want to give back a large portion of the 1997 surplus with a one-time break.

Massachusetts ends its fiscal year on June 30, and in 1996, it used a smaller surplus to repay $150 million to its citizens. Both officials also want to cut the personal income tax to 5.0 percent from 5.95 percent.

Malone, who forecast a $600 million to $700 million surplus in fiscal 1997, would give residents about $300 million, deposit the same amount in the Rainy Day Fund -- a cushion that can be used if the economy stumbles -- and spend another $100 million or so on projects that lawmakers all approve.
The acting governor projects a smaller, $300 million to $400 million surplus because he expects the legislature to use about $200 million for one-time, capital projects.

Cellucci, who noted the state did not have a stabilization fund in the last recession, sees the Rainy Day Fund, which now has about $600 million, ending fiscal 1997 with over $700 million, and projects it will have more than $800 million next year.
